19q0yjo:234: The real issue is not whether AI causes literal brain damage, but how you use it determines whether it helps or harms your mind. The MIT study's key finding: when students were asked to use ChatGPT without special prompting, they took shortcuts to get answers. Even though students thought they learned a lot from ChatGPT's help, they actually learned less—scoring 17% lower on final exams than classmates who didn't use ChatGPT. AI is trained to provide help and answer questions, and this default mode bypasses the (sometimes unpleasant) mental effort that produces learning.

1kadmwv:318: In education, the key scenario where AI use hurts learning is when trying to learn or synthesize new knowledge. If you outsource thinking to AI instead of doing the work yourself, you miss the learning opportunity. Unguided ChatGPT use dropped Turkish high school students' exam scores by 17%, because AI defaults to giving answers rather than guiding students to think on their own. But when AI is used with teacher guidance and sound teaching principles, the results are very different: the World Bank's six-week ChatGPT tutoring program in Nigeria (with teacher guidance) found "effects exceeding some of the most effective educational interventions"; Harvard found that carefully prompted AI tutors outperformed active classrooms in a large physics course experiment; Stanford's large programming course study found ChatGPT use improved grades; a Malaysian study found AI combined with teacher guidance and solid pedagogy led to more learning.

tffo1w:253: People often ask "Does AI harm the brain?" The question itself reveals a deep fear of AI's capabilities. MIT Media Lab's "Your Brain on ChatGPT" study has been widely misunderstood—it involved only a small group of college students assigned to write alone, use Google, or use ChatGPT for essays. Students using ChatGPT were less engaged, remembered less, performed worse when rewriting four months later, and showed reduced EEG activity. But the study showed no "brain damage"—Plato thought writing would weaken intelligence, and when phones appeared, some worried that not memorizing phone numbers would make us stupid. Tech anxiety is nothing new.
